item.title: Fixing x86-64 Call Overflow in PIE Executables: PLT vs GOT Strategies
item.description:
“Fixing x86-64 Call Overflow in PIE Executables: PLT vs GOT Strategies”

How can we properly resolve calls to external dynamic library functions (puts in this case) when compiling with PIE enabled, and what are the alternatives to avoid this 32-bit address space limitation?

Analyzing the Default PIE Behavior and Overflow

By default, recent gcc compilers generate PIE code. When an assembly routine compiled under these settings uses a simple call puts, the linker generates a R_X86_64_PC32 relocation. At runtime, the dynamic linker attempts to resolve puts directly to its address in libc and fix up the relative call. If the distance between the call site and the resolved puts address exceeds the 32-bit signed offset limit ($2^{31}$), the relocation fails or causes a warning, leading the call to jump to an incorrect address because only the lower 32 bits of the target address are correct.

item.title: Why is 16-byte Stack Alignment Crucial for SSE2 Vectorization and x86-64?
item.description:
“Why is 16-byte Stack Alignment Crucial for SSE2 Vectorization and x86-64?”

Why does the x86-64 System V ABI and Windows x64 mandate 16-byte stack alignment, especially when it seems to facilitate efficient stack allocation for data types like long double and __m128i, and local arrays to enable SSE2 vectorization? What are the underlying technical reasons and potential implications of not adhering to this alignment?

At its core, the requirement for 16-byte stack alignment on x86-64 is deeply intertwined with the capabilities and requirements of the Streaming SIMD Extensions 2 (SSE2) instruction set, which is standard on all x86-64 processors. SSE2 introduces 128-bit registers (__m128) that can hold multiple data elements, enabling SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations. For these operations to execute efficiently, the data they operate on must be aligned to specific boundaries.

item.title: x86 Assembly Registers: EAX, AX, AH, AL Explained
item.description:
“x86 Assembly Registers: EAX, AX, AH, AL Explained”

When working with x86 assembly, a common point of exploration involves the relationship between the 32-bit EAX register and its constituent parts: AX (the lower 16 bits), AH (the upper 8 bits of AX), and AL (the lower 8 bits of AX). How do these registers interact, and what are the implications of accessing them individually?

The structure of these registers is hierarchical. EAX represents the full 32-bit value. AX is a subset, containing the lower 16 bits of EAX. AL is the least significant byte (bits 0-7) of AX (and thus of EAX), while AH comprises bits 8-15 of AX (the upper half of AX, or the second byte of EAX).

item.title: x86 PUSH Operation: Does Immediate Size Determine Stack Push Size

“x86 PUSH Operation: Does Immediate Size Determine Stack Push Size”

A frequent point of confusion in x86 assembly programming revolves around the PUSH instruction: Does the numerical value provided to PUSH dictate how many bytes are written to the stack, or is it strictly determined by the instruction’s operand size context?

The direct answer is that the size of the immediate value that fits within an imm8 (immediate 8-bit) encoding does not dictate the operand size for the PUSH operation. The stack pointer (ESP/RSP) is decremented by the established operand-size for that specific instruction execution mode, irrespective of how small the immediate value is.

The rep movsb instruction in x86 assembly has a storied past regarding performance. While once advised against, architectural improvements have made it a contender again. This exploration delves into when and why rep movsb might be beneficial, its technical underpinnings, and how it stacks up against modern memcpy implementations.

Historical Context and Official Guidance

Historically, advice surrounding rep movsb has been inconsistent. Early guidance often suggested avoiding it or using it with extreme caution. For instance, pre-Ivy Bridge guides recommended careful usage. More recent Intel optimization manuals offer nuanced advice. For example, a June 2016 guide stated that the specific variant of rep movsb is chosen at execution time based on data layout, alignment, and the counter value (ECX). It suggested using MOVSB/STOSB with REP for counter values less than or equal to three. However, this recommendation for tiny counts seems counterintuitive given the instruction’s startup latency.

item.title: Fixing Bootloader Issues: Segment Offset and Sector Read Errors
item.description:
“Fixing Bootloader Issues: Segment Offset and Sector Read Errors”

When developing bootloaders, particularly in 16-bit x86 assembly, several subtle issues can prevent your code from executing correctly. Two common hurdles involve how the kernel is loaded into memory (segment:offset) and the correct parameters for reading sectors from disk using BIOS interrupt INT 13h.

The Segment:Offset Conundrum

A fundamental aspect of 16-bit memory addressing is the segment:offset pair. Memory is accessed using a 20-bit physical address, derived from a 16-bit segment register and a 16-bit offset. The formula is Physical Address = (Segment * 16) + Offset. In assembly, multiplying a segment by 16 is equivalent to a left bit shift by 4 (segment << 4).

item.title: Fixing SIGSEGV: 16-Byte Stack Alignment Issues in x86-64 Assembly
item.description:
“Fixing SIGSEGV: 16-Byte Stack Alignment Issues in x86-64 Assembly”

Encountering a SIGSEGV (Segmentation Fault) can be a cryptic hurdle in low-level programming. One frequent culprit, particularly in x86-64 architecture when interacting with modern C library functions like printf or scanf, is insufficient stack alignment. This post delves into the reasons behind this requirement and provides actionable solutions.

The x86-64 System V ABI (Application Binary Interface) mandates a 16-byte stack alignment for function calls. This means that before a function makes another call, the stack pointer (RSP) must be a multiple of 16. Why this strictness? Modern compilers, like GCC, increasingly leverage advanced instruction sets such as SSE2 for performance. Instructions like movaps (move aligned packed single-precision floats) require their operands, including memory locations on the stack, to be 16-byte aligned. Failure to meet this alignment results in a SIGSEGV.

Q: What are the primary considerations for loading static addresses into registers on x86-64

ANS: On x86-64, most immediates and displacements are kept at 32-bits to conserve code size. This affects how static addresses are loaded into registers. Using full 64-bit addresses can significantly increase the instruction cache footprint and fetch/decode bandwidth, impacting performance. Understanding these trade-offs is crucial for efficient code generation. For more on x86 architecture, see the x86 tag wiki .

Q: How does LEA with RIP-relative addressing work for static data

ANS: RIP-relative LEA is the standard and efficient method. It uses a 32-bit relative displacement from the instruction pointer’s current position, similar to how jmp or call instructions operate. This approach can access any static data within .data, .bss, .rodata, or functions in .text, provided the total size of static code and data stays within the typical 2GiB limit. This method is compatible with address space layout randomization (ASLR).
